chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Husayn ibn Musa, from Fuzayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام), who said:

'What would he care — the one whom Allah causes to recognise this matter (al-Wilayah) — if he were to be upon the summit of a mountain, eating from the vegetation of the earth, until death comes to him?'

key_terms.الْمَوْتُ: death — the natural terminus of earthly life, presented here as inconsequential when weighed against the gift of wilayah
key_terms.عَرَّفَهُ: caused him to recognise / made him aware — denotes Allah's direct act of granting the servant true ma'rifah (gnosis) of the Imams' authority
key_terms.قُلَّةِ جَبَلٍ: the summit of a mountain — a vivid image of total societal isolation and remoteness from worldly comfort and community
key_terms.نَبَاتِ الْأَرْضِ: the vegetation of the earth — bare, unprocessed sustenance symbolising complete material austerity
key_terms.هَذَا الْأَمْرَ: this matter — a standing Shia technical expression for wilayah: the recognition of and allegiance to the divinely appointed Imams
key_terms.يُبَالِي: cares / is concerned — used here negatively ('does not care at all'), expressing total indifference to worldly hardship on account of a greater gift

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir (AS) say about the spiritual sufficiency of recognising wilayah?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (عليه السلام) declares that whoever has been granted by Allah the recognition of wilayah — the divine guardianship and authority of the Imams — is entirely indifferent to worldly circumstances, even if he lives alone on a mountaintop subsisting on wild vegetation until death. The hadith establishes that the gift of ma'rifah of 'this matter' is so transcendent in worth that no material deprivation can diminish it, and the one who possesses it is spiritually complete regardless of outward condition.
